3. It is stated in the application that the detenu had actively participated is the student politics and democratic movements during his student-life; that he obtained his MA degree from the University of Dhaka and was called to the Bar as a Barrister-at-Law in the year 1966 and was enrolled as an Advocate of this Court in 1966, that he wrote a few books of which "Bangladesh : Constitutional quest for Autonomy" and "Bangladesh : Era of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman" are prominent; that he was elected as a Member of Parliament in 1979 and also twice thereafter; that he was appointed Adviser of the President in 1977 and elevated to the post of Minister in 1978 and thereafter he became Deputy Prime Minister, then Prime Minister and ultimately he was appointed Vice-President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh on 12.6.89; that he remained the Vice-President of the country till he voluntarily resigned on December 6, 1990, in whose place the Chief Justice of Bangladesh was appointed as Vice-President and who is now acting as President of Bangladesh as head of the Caretaker Government; that an order of detention under section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 (hereinafter referred to as the said Act) was passed by the respondent No. 2 on 11.12.90, directing to detain the detenu in his house at Gulshan for 120 days for public safety and maintenance of public order; that the said order of detention has been annexed with the application and marked as Annexure-A, that the subsequent arrest and detention of the detenu under section 3(1)(a) of the said Act is not only unlawful and illegal but it is malafide and it has been made purely for co-lateral purposes to creates hurdle on the part of the detenu to contest the ensuing election of the Parliament, that the ground of detention of the detenu in the present context of facts has become totally non-existent and there is no reasons to pass such an order of detention which is malafide, illegal and unlawful; that the reason for detention as stated in the impugned order does not come within the scope of prejudicial activities and there was no material before the Government to pass such an order of detention; that on 24.12.90 the grounds for detention under section 3 of the said Act have been served upon the detenu, the copy of which is annexed with the application and marked as Annexure 'B'. That the grounds communicated to the detenu do not constitute any prejudicial act on the part of the detention; that the grounds are vague, indefinite, illusory and non-existent; that the ground No. 1 does not and cannot constitute any prejudicial act within the meaning of the said act; that as to ground No. 2 with regard to Press interview the detenu did not violate any law nor had he anything to do with the incident which occurred on 10th December, 1990. That ground Nos. 3 and 4 are not only vague and indefinite but also baseless and motivated and that the detenu voluntarily resigned from the post of Vice-President to enable to form the present Caretaker Government and that the whole purpose of this order of detention is to prevent the detenu from contesting the ensuing Parliamentary election. 

 4. That an affidavit-in-opposition on behalf of the respondents, affirmed by a Deputy Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs of the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, has been filed by the respondents contending, inter alia, that the detenu had a strong background of political capability and such capability is sufficient enough to utilise entrenched support available to the Jatiya Party and the earlier regime in the administration in order to destabilise the present situation and thereby to endanger public safety and public order and as such the detention of the detenu has become necessary with a view to preserve and protect the public safety and public order for having free and fair election in the country; that the detenu was removed on the 2nd January, 1986 from the post of Minister and he was tried before a Special Martial Law Court under Martial Law Regulation 11 and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 10 years and also to pay a fine of Tk. 3 (three) lakhs, in default to suffer imprisonment for three years more and subsequently this was reviewed by the erstwhile Chief Martial Law Administrator and on review he was released from jail; that on being released from jail the detenu was actively associated with BNP leader Begum Khaleda Zia but thereafter joined the Cabinet of former President Ershad and subsequently elevated to the post of Vice-President; that on analysis of the background of the detenu it shows that the detenu assumed different colors at different times with the change of political situation for acquiring power and in doing so he was widely reputed as a corrupt man which has created a strong political agitation against him; that it was not correct that the detenu resigned voluntarily on 6.12.90 and the chronology of political movement would show that the detenu had to resign due to political agitation launched by the people, restoration of democratic rights and for holding a and free election under the neutral Government; that during the tenure of his office the detenu had acquired the reputation as a corrupt man, that he was alleged to have adopted corrupt practice and favouritism, that in support of the allegation of corrupt practice by the detenu certain weekly magazine has been annexed with the affidavit which have been marked as Annexures X and Y series; that the detenu was detained for his prejudicial activities against public safety and maintenance of public order; that the detenu has a powerful background to destabilise the present situation and thereby he is quite capable to endanger public safety and public order; that there are sufficient materials before the detaining authority necessitating to pass the order of detention for preventing him from acting in a manner prejudicial to public safety and public order; that the detenu has been detained under one ground alone i.e. for maintenance of public safety and public order; that the detenu while staying in his own house after his resignation made a statement in the 'Morning Sun' on 8.12.90 which was published on 9.12.90 which shows that the detenu was maintaining a close liason with the former President as a result of which a section of the public was agitated and attacked his house on 10.12.90 by throwing cocktail showing public agitation against the detenu and thereby endangered public safety and public order; that the paper cuttings of the statement of the dam have been annexed with the affidavit and marked as Annexures Z and Z(1); that the dam was so long absconding and he was arrested on 20.12.90 from House No. 5, Road No. 7, Baridhara, Gulshan which, belonged to one Shamim Rahman Ansari who is connected with Beximco Company and the said. Beximco Company was widely reputed for having close association with the former President for which Beximco Office at Road No. 2 Dhanmondi was attacked by the picketers during the public agitation on 27.10. 90; that after making the statement to the Morning Sun the detenu was not found in his Gulshan residence and he was found hiding at Baridhara wherefrom he was arrested; that during the period of hiding the detenu seemed to have made several telephone calls, local as well as international, calling on sensitive officers of the Ministry and foreign embassies and this could be constituted overt acts on the part of the detenu to destabilise the present Caretaker Government by mobilising the erstwhile regime; that the statement of the detenu in the Morning Sun was placed before the former President and the former President has given a telephonic interviews to the correspondent of British Broadcasting Corporation and the said interview led to the public agitation and that the detenu was trying to mobilise support of sensitive persons to destabilise the Caretaker Government and thereby acted prejudicially to endanger public safety and maintenance of public order. 

 5. The petitioner filed an affidavit-in-reply to the affidavit-in-opposition of the respondents wherein it has been stated that the alleged materials mentioned in the affidavit-in-opposition are all of subsequent dates after the order of detention was passed; that the alleged background of political capability cannot be a ground for detention of the detenu under the Act; that the different paper cuttings are all extraneous matter of subsequent dates and as such these have no bearing on the order of detention and that the detenu was detained for co-lateral purpose and not for preventing him from doing any prejudicial act; that the petitioner reiterated his statement made in the application and further stated that the policy of the neutral Government is to allow every citizen to participate in the ensuing parliamentary election irrespective of his party affiliation and the detenu is contesting from two constituencies from the district of Noakhali. By a supplementary affidavit filed by the respondents it. has been stated that from the statement issued by the Acting President of the Jatiya Party it is clear that the leaders of Jatiya Party and its associates are making desperate efforts to destabilise the present Central Government which provides a bonafide impression that the detenu is likely to endanger maintenance of public order and public safety. In support of the statement extracts of the weekly magazine 'Purbabhash' dated 22.1.91 and Daily Hongkong Standard dated 28.1.91 have been annexed with the affidavit as Annexures z-5 and z-6. In reply to this the petitioner by an affidavit-in-reply stated that what was stated by the Acting President of the Jatiya Party or what has been published in the papers those have no relevancy for the disposal of the case and all these go to show that the detenu has been detained without any material available on the date of the order of detention and that to justify the illegal detention the respondents are trying to introduce all irrelevant and extraneous matters. 

 6. By a subsequent supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of the respondents it has been stated that the detenu had never voluntarily resigned from the post of Vice-President, rather he was opposed to the installation of the present Caretaker Government which is evident from his interview with the correspondent of British Broadcasting Corporation on 2.12.90 and 3.12.90 and the relevant documents as mentioned by Radio Bangladesh and the relevant document are annexed therewith and marked as Annexures Z-7 and Z-8. 

 10. Thus it is for the High Court Division to satisfy itself that the detenu is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner. The theory of subjective satisfaction as propounded by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Liversidge Vs. Sir John Anderson and another (1942 AC 206) is being followed in the Indian Jurisdiction so long; but since 1962 there was a radical change by Article 98(2)(b)(i) of the 1962 Constitution of Pakistan in a language substantially similar to the provision of Article 102 (2)(b)(i) of our Constitution and the Supreme Court of Pakistan in a series of decisions namely in the case of Golam Mani Vs. Government of West Pakistan (19 DLR (SC) 403), Mir Abdul Baqi Baluch Vs. Government of Pakistan (20 DLR (SC) 294) Government of West Pakistan Vs. Begum Agha Abdul Karim Shorish Kashmiri (21 DLR 1) held that the constitution has cast a heavy duty upon the court to satisfy itself that there is a competent law authorising the detention and the officers issuing an order have been lawfully vested with the power, that the action of the detaining authority is not malafide and that the action has not been taken upon extraneous or irrelevant considerations and without proper application of mind. 

 11. Our Appellate Division in the case of Abdul Latif Mirza Vs. Government of Bangladesh and others (31 DLR (AD) 1) interpreted the provision of Article 102(2)(b)(i) of the Constitution of Bangladesh along with the provision of section 3 of the Special Powers Act under which the detaining authority passed an order of detention; and held that the High Court Division is to be satisfied that the person in detention is not so held either without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner and interpreted the phases stating that the expression "without lawful authority" comprehends all questions of the competency or the vires of an enactment, that is, there must be a competent law empowering an authority to detain a person, and empowered authority acting under the conferred powers must be vested with that power by law and the expression "in an unlawful manner" comprehends the circumstances of the detention as to whether the action is malafide or colorable exercise of statutory powers or the action taken upon extraneous or irrelevant considerations and whether action is taken upon with the application of mind of the detaining authority. Considering the provision of section 3 of the Special Powers Act it has been held by their Lordships that section 3 standing by itself emphasises of the detaining authority to act in purely subjective manner but the Constitution has given a mandate to the High Court Division to satisfy itself, as a judicial authority that the detention is a lawful detention; and giving a harmonious interpretation it has been held that "the detaining authority's satisfaction is to a great extent subjective, but the order of detaining authority must be based on some materials which will satisfy a reasonable person that a conclusion could be so drawn on such materials," As to the adequacy or the sufficiency of the materials it must depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division further pointed out that although the satisfaction of the detaining authority has got an objective basis, it has got a subjective feature as to the adequacy or sufficiency of the grounds which are beyond the purview of judicial review and the court cannot substitute its own satisfaction or opinion in place of that of the detaining authority. 

 12. The same view has been reiterated by our Appellate Division in the case of Mrs. Sajeda Parvin Vs. Government of Bangladesh, 40 DLR (AD) 178. In this case their Lordships of the Appellate Division have pointed out that the language of Article 102 of our Constitution and that of Article 98 of 1962 Constitution of Pakistan is radically different from Article 176 of the 1956 Constitution of Pakistan and Article 226 of the Indian Constitution and held that "the court is to satisfy itself that the person is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner, the court is enjoined to consider the materials. What the court is concerned with, is to see that the executive or administrative authority had before it sufficient materials upon which a reasonable person could have come to the conclusion that the requirements of law were satisfied." 

 15. It appears that the detaining authority passed the order under section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act 1974 being satisfied that it was necessary for the maintenance of public safety and public order that the detenu should be detained. The grounds for detention which was communicated to the detenu on 24.12.90 Annexure 'B' reads as follows: 

 16. It has been contended by Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, that the Court must be satisfied that there are materials on the basis of which the detaining authority passed the order of detention and that the ground must be related to the purpose of the statute and there must be a nexus between the order of detention and the ground furnished by the detaining authority. According to Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq, there are three grounds as mentioned in paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 of Annexure B. The first of which is vague and indefinite and referred to the likelihood of an attacked on the life of the detenu; the second one is with regard to the statement given to the reporter of Daily Morning Sun by the detenu on 8.12.90 and an incident that occurred on 10.12.90 in the residence of the detenu for which the safety of the life of the detenu would have been affected had house been present at his house at the time of the occurrence; the 3rd ground mentioned therein is that the detenu went into hiding and this may be for the safety and security of his life. According to Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq, these are three independent grounds which led to the conclusion mentioned in paragraph 4 i.e. for maintenance of public safety and public order. But, according to the learned Advocate, those are merely disturbance of law and order leading to disorder which is not necessarily for prejudicial activities. He has referred to the case of Ranabir Das Vs. Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs (28 DLR 48) in support of his contention wherein it has been held that contravention of law always affects the order but before it can be said to affect public order, it must affect the community or public at large; mere disturbance of law and order leading to disorder is not necessarily sufficient for taking notion for prejudicial activities. In this connection he has also referred to the case of Pushker Mukharjee and others vs. The Slate of West Bengal (AIR 1970 (SC) 852) wherein it has been held that a mere disturbance of law and order leading to disorder is not necessarily sufficient for action under the preventive detention but a disturbance which will affect public order comes within the ambit of public order. According to Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq, the first ground cannot constitute any prejudicial act on the part of the detenu within the meaning of section 2(i) of the Special Powers Act and the order of detention was passed only to protect the detenu which is the duty of every Government to preserve the life and property of every citizen. According to the learned Advocate, the mere giving of an interview with the reporters of newspapers cannot be treated as a prejudicial act as it does not violate any law; and the incident that occurred on 10.12.90 at the residence of the detenu was an act of a handful of persons politically opposed to the detenu and the damage of the house of the detenu by a few miscreants cannot be regarded as endangering public safety and public order but it would be a matter of law and order only. Further, the mere absconding or hiding on the part of the detenu cannot be regarded as a valid ground for detention. 

 17. The learned Attorney-General, on the other hand, has contended that the reading of Annexure it would appear that there is only one ground for detention of the detenu which is for preventing the detenu from endangering public safety or the maintenance of public order. According to the learned Attorney-General, paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 of Annex\i, 'B' are pieces of evidence or materials which led to the conclusion of the detaining authority as mentioned in paragraph 4. The learned Attorney-General further submitted that paragraphs 1, 2, 3 and 4 were expressed in disjunctive manner but they constitute a single ground. In support of his contention the learned Attorney-General has referred to the case of The. State of Bombay Vs. Atma Ram Shridhar Veidya (AIR 1951 (SC) 157) wherein it has been pointed out that the grounds have formed the basis of satisfaction when formulated, are bound to contain certain facts but mostly they are deduction from facts. Ordinarily the ground in the sense is conclusion drawn by the authorities which indicate the kind of prejudicial act the detenu is suspected of being engaged in and that will be sufficient to enable him to make representation. According to the learned Attorney- General, Annexure B contained only one conclusion drawn from the facts stated in paragraphs 1, 2 and 3. It is submitted by the learned Attorney-General that it would appear from the ground there is a public resentment against the detenu for his alleged corrupt practice and abuse of power, that there was continuous agitation by the public at large immediately after the announcement of resignation of the former President on 4.12.90 for which there was probability of disturbance of public order even leading to attack on the life of the detenu; that as a matter of fact in view of his statement in the Morning Sun a section of public became excited and attacked his residence by exploding cocktail and damaging the house, and had the detenu been present at his house at that time there was likelihood of danger to his life and that there was a public resentment and hatred for his going into hiding as a result of which there is likelihood of serious disturbance to public safety and public order. According to the learned Attorney-General, paragraph 1 of Annexure B has a reference to the antecedent past history and past conduct of the detenu and this background of the detenu can be the basis of his detention. In support of his contention the .learned Attorney-General has referred to the case of Nurunnahar Begum Vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others (29 DLR 372) wherein it has been held that preventive detention is called for only when certain prejudicial activities create impression in the mind of the detaining authority, that if the subject is allowed to remain free when he is likely to act prejudicially endangering public safety and these apprehensions can be formed, on the basis of antecedent history of the detenu. He has also referred to the case of Keshave Nilkanth Joglekar Vs. The Commissioner of Police, Greater Bombay and others (AIR 1957 (SC) 28) wherein it has been held that past activities of a person can be a ground for detention because what a person is likely to do in future can only be a matter of inference from various circumstances, and his past record will be valuable and often the only record on which it could be made. He has also referred to the case of Nagen Murmu Vs. The State of West Bengal (AIR 1973 (SC) 844) wherein it has been held that the past conduct antecedent history of a person can appropriately be taken into account in making a detention order. The learned Attorney-General, therefore, submitted that having regard to the antecedent past history of the detenu, his statement in the daily Morning Sun and his absconding along with the overall prevailing situation in the country justified the notion of the detaining authority in passing the impugned order of detention for the maintenance of public safety and public order. I find force in this contention of the learned Attorney-General. It is an isolated act which might lead to law and order situation, but the several facts stated in the ground of detention in the background of the overall prevailing situation of the country is to be considered as the basis for passing the impugned order of detention. 

 20. Where the order of detention is challenged under Article 102(2)(b)(i) of the Constitution, the High Court Division is to be satisfied that the person in custody is not so held without lawful authority or in any unlawful manner. It is now a settled position of law that the constitutional obligation imposed upon this Court by Article 102 (2)(b)(i) is clearly to make an objective assessment of the materials on which the necessary satisfaction of the detaining authority had been based and to be satisfied that an average prudent man could reasonably be so satisfied. In this connection reference may be made to the decision in the case of Abdul Latif Mirza Vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 31 DLR (AD) 1 in which their Lordships of the Appellate Division held as under: 

 The Government, in exercise of its powers under section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act 1974 ordered detention of Mr. Moudud Ahmed, former Vice-President of the Republic for 120 days "for public safety and maintenance of public order" without recording its satisfaction in express words that the detenu was required to be detained for preventing him from doing any prejudicial act. Section 3(1)(a) of the Act reads thus: 

 "3(1) The Government may, if satisfied with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act it is necessary so to do, make an order- 

 Here we are concerned with a part of section 2 (f)(iii) which states that "prejudicial act" means any act which is intended or likely to endanger public safety or maintenance of public order. The act of the detenu unless intended or likely to endanger public safety or maintenance of public order cannot be the basis for an order under section 3(i)(a). If in any situation the maintenance of public order or public safety is endangered or disturbed by the acts of person of persons other than the detenu, the latter cannot be detained under that section. Since the impugned order of detention does not expressly record the satisfaction of the Government to the effect that the detention of the detenu is necessary with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act or any act which is intended or likely to endanger public safety or maintenance or public order, the detention of the detenu is ex facie illegal and without lawful authority. 

 21. Mr. Rafiqul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, has submitted that there is no basis for the 3 grounds on which the order of detention has been Made and that these grounds are vague, indefinite, irrelevant and extraneous. Mr. Aminul Huq, the learned Attorney General, on the other hand, has contended that the detenu had been detained under one ground alone and that paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 of the Annexure-'B' constitute different pieces of evidence by which the Authority making the order came to the conclusion that the detenu was acting in a manner prejudicial to public safety and maintenance of public order. To substantiate his contention as to only one ground, he has referred to the words "এবং" (and) appearing at the end of the paragraphs 1-3 which show that the evidence stated therein constituted only one ground as stated in paragraph 4 that the detention of the detenu was necessary in the interest of public safety and public order. I am unable to accept this contention of the learned Attorney General as the expressions ১। “নিম্নলিখিত কারণসমূহের” 

 22. The first ground relates to the alleged corruption and abuse of power by the detenu which generated public anger against him and that his detention was necessary for his own safety which was likely to be jeopardised by the spontaneous attack of the people on the supporters of the former regime. If the detenu had practiced corruption or committed criminal misconduct by abusing his position while in office, the law would take its own course. The use of the extraordinary power of preventive detention contained in the Special Powers Act for purposes for which ordinary law is sufficient is a glaring proof of abuse of statutory powers by the detaining authority. Moreover the alleged corruption by itself would not come within the definition of prejudicial act as defined in section 2(f). The alleged corruption and abuse of power having been already committed, there would arise no necessity for detention of the detenu to prevent him from prejudicing the economic or financial interest of the state. From the perusal of this ground it is evident that impugned order of detention was passed to protect or save the detenu from attack by the people and for the safety of his life but it was not intended to prevent him from doing any prejudicial act. No person can be kept in protective custody for his own safety and such ground falls outside the ambit of the Special Powers Act. 

 23. As regards the 2nd ground it may be stated that the press interview given by the detenu on 8.12.90 which was published on the following day in the English Daily "Morning Sun" (Annexure '2' on the affidavit-in-opposition) does not contain anything which violated any law, nor it contained my provocative statement to endanger public safety or maintenance of public order. In that interview the detenu only emphasised that the caretaker Government should maintain neutrality and ensure the participation of all political parties including Jatiya Party in the coming election. The attack and damage caused to the house of the detenu on 10.12.90 allegedly by a section of the public cannot be the result or consequence of the said press interview as the same was very innocent. The Government, in all fairness, should have taken action according to law against persons who were responsible for the said incident and such undesirable incident should not have-been made an excuse for passing of the order of detention. Such a press interview by a political person like the detenu who till recently held the office of the Vice President of the Republic cannot be construed to be a prejudicial act when the Jatiya Party, to which the detenu belongs, or its members had not been debarred from participating in the parliamentary poll scheduled to be held on the 27th of this month. The detenu, in my view, has got legal right to make statement as reported in the 'Morning Sun' when the freedom of press and freedom of speech are guaranteed under Article 39 of the Constitution of Bangladesh. This ground also shows that the detention of the detenu was necessitated for the safely of his life and not to prevent him from doing any prejudicial act and thus this also falls outside the ambit of the Special Powers Act. 

 24. The 3rd ground relates to the hiding of the detenu which resulted in public dissatisfaction and hatred against him and which was likely to endanger public safety and public order. The order of detention was passed on 11.12.90 and the detenu was arrested on 20.12.90. If the detaining authority had reason to believe that the detenu had absconded or was concealing himself so that the order of detention could not be executed, the Government could take action in accordance with the provision of section 7 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 which reads thus : 

 "7. If the Government or a District Magistrate or an Additional District Magistrate mentioned in section 2(3), as the case may be, has reason to believe that a person in respect of whom a detention order has been made has absconded or is concealing himself so that the order cannot be executed, it or he may— 

 25. The Government, it is evident, did not take any action in the light of section 7 till the arrest of the detenu. The hiding of the dctenu does not by itself constitute a prejudicial act. The act of absconding it no doubt a relevant piece of evidence under section 8 of the Evidence Act, but its value would always depend on the circumstances of such case. Mere absconding or hiding does not necessarily lead to a firm conclusion of guilty mind of the detenu. Even an innocent person may feel panicky or try to evade arrest when unjustifiably suspected of grave offence or of indulging in prejudicial act. The hiding of the detenu in a house at Baridhara might have been prompted by his instinct of self preservation. 

 27. It has been contended by the learned Attorney General that the past conduct or antecedent history of a person can be taken into account in making an order of detention under the Special Powers Act. Without disputing the correctness of the contention, it may be said that such conduct or antecedent should ordinarily proximate in point of time and should have rational connection with the conclusion that the detention of the person is necessary. It has been repeatedly stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that the detenu had a strong background of political capability and such capability is sufficient enough to utilise entrenched support available to Jatiya Party and earlier regime in the administration and other areas to destabilise the present situation or the present caretaker Government and that in such situation the detention of the detenu was necessary to preserve and protect the public safety and public f order for holding free and fair election in the country. No such ground finds place in the grounds communicated to the detenu and such ground was not before the detaining authority at the time of passing of the impugned order of detention. This has been introduced in the affidavit- in-opposition to show that the detenu was indulging in activities which could come within the definition of prejudicial acts. This appears to be an after thought and a fiction of imagination. The order of detention, it is evident, has been passed in colourable exercise of authority and it has been vitiated by irrelevant grounds. This court cannot go beyond the grounds embodied in annexure-B on which the satisfaction of the detaining authority was based. 

 28. The object of enactment of the Special Powers Act, 1974 was to provide for special measures for the prevention of certain prejudicial invitees, for more speedy trial and effective punishment of certain grave offences and for matter connected therewith. Since the order of detention has been made without recording the satisfaction of the detaining authority that the detenu was required to be detained with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act, the order of detention must be held to be malafide as it was made contrary to the object and purposes of the Act. The grounds of detention show that the detaining authority was influenced by irrelevant grounds and extraneous consideration and there was no sufficient material before it to come to the conclusion that the detention of the detenu was necessary with a view to preventing him from doing any act which is intended or likely to endanger a public safety or maintenance of public order. The impugned order of detention was passed without any valid ground and without application of the mind of the detaining authority. 

 In view of the difference of opinion let the matter be placed before the learned Acting Chief Justice for necessary order. 

 32. The matter was heard by a Division Bench of this court comprising IU Sarkar and B Zaman, JJ. After hearing the learned counsels for the parties my brother IU Sarkar, I took the view "that the detaining authority had sufficient materials for passing the order of detention under section 3 of the Act for the purpose of preventive detention of the &term for preventing him from endangering public safety and public order which is a prejudicial act within the meaning of section 3(0(111) of the Special Powers, Act, 1974", while my brother B Zaman, J opined that the order of detention is ex facie illegal as the impugned order does not expressly record the satisfaction of the Government to the affect that the detention of the detenu is necessary with a view to preventing him from doing any act prejudicial to public safety and public order. He was also of the view that the detaining authority failed to produce any material on the basis of which a prudent man could be satisfied as to the necessity of detaining the detcnu for the purpose of preventing him from acting in a manner prejudicial to public safety or public order and that the grounds of detention had no rational connection with the object of detention. There being thus a difference of opinion as to the validity of the detention, the learned Chief Justice by an order dated 16.2.1991, referred the matter to me for hearing and disposal. 

 34. On 11th December, 1990 the Government, in exercise of the power under section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act, passed an order directing that the detenu be detained for a period of 120 days from the date of the service of the order as it appeared to the satisfaction of the Government that his detention was necessary for the maintenance of public safety and public order. In pursuance of the said order the detenu was apprehended on 20th December 1990 and on the 24th December, 1990 the grounds for his detention were supplied to him. The English rendering of the grounds conveyed to the detenu runs thus: 

 a) That the public at large have a resentment in their minds against you as one indulging in corruption and misuse of power and with the announcement of the erstwhile President on the 4th of December, 1990 of his resignation a large number of people got down on the streets and made inroads upon the persons and institutions connected with the previous Government and spontaneous attack was conducted by the people upon the institution which is the expression of their pent up wrath and on account of the situation described in this first paragraph there was apprehension of attempt on your life, and 

 b) That on 8th December, 1990 last in your private interview with the journalist of "Morning Sun" in your house you had made various inciting statements about the future of Jatiya Party and yourself and also about your politics which has been published in the "Morning Sun". As a result a section of the public became incited and damaged your house by cocktail burst on 10.12.1990. Had you been present in the house after that, it appears, your life would have been jeopardized and. 

 d) That on over-all consideration of the circumstances stated in the above paragraphs and the situation obtaining in the country it appears to the satisfaction of the Government that your detention under section 3(1) of the Special Powers Act. 1974 is necessary in the interest of public safety and the maintenance of public order. 

 f) You are further informed that you have a right to make a representation to the Government against the order of detention made against you." 

 36. In response to the Rule Nisi issued by this Court Major (Retd) Chowdhury Montajuddin Ahmed, Deputy Secretary in the Ministry of Home Affairi of the Government filed affidavit-in-opposition, in para 4 of which it is averred that "the detenu had a strong background of political capability and such capability is sufficient enough to utilise entrenched support available to Jatiya Party and earlier regime in the administration and other areas to destabilise the present situation and thereby it can endanger public safety and public order and as such for the time being his detention has become necessary with a view to preserve and protect the public safety and public order for having free and fair election in the country by the present caretaker Government." 

 37. The gravamen of the petitioner's grievance is that the impugned preventive action of the Government is beyond the purview of the said Act and hence violative of Article 32 of the Constitution which inhibits blanket and arbitrary deprivation of a person's liberty by authority. 

 Section 3(1) (a) then lays down that the Government, may if satisfied with respect to any person that with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act it is necessary so to do, make an order directing that such person be detained". 

 39. The said provision manifestly requires that before the Government can pass an order of detention it must be satisfied with respect to the individual person that his activities are directed against the object mentioned in the section and that it is necessary to prevent him from acting in such a manner. While empowering the Government to pass a preventive order the section thus appears to have expressly made it a part of its duty to satisfy itself about the existence of what the lawmakers regard as condition precedent to the exercise of that power. An order being indicative of the state of the mind of the authority making it, the concerned order of detention must expressly state that the Government is satisfied that it is necessary to make the order to prevent the individual from doing any prejudicial act. If the order is silent in that respect the detention will undoubtedly be not in terms of the section. 

 40. The question then immediately arises whether the Government complied with the requirements of the section in passing the impugned order of detention. The first ground of attack against the validity of the order is that the detaining authority failed to record its satisfaction that it was considered necessary to make the order of detention with a view to preventing the detenu from doing any prejudicial act. The order of detention reads thus: 

 41. Obviously, there is nothing in the order to even suggest that the Government was satisfied that it was necessary to make the order of detention with a view to preventing the detenu from doing any prejudicial act which is the sine qua non for exercise of the power under section 3(1) of the said Act. This omission undoubtedly constitutes a serious infirmity which has inevitably taken the order of detention out of the ambit of the section. Another ground of challenge urged on behalf of the petitioner is that the order of detention ex facie shows that the detenu was detained simply in the interest of public safety and the maintenance of public order. Section 3(1) read with section 2(f) of the Act clearly prescribes certain specific grounds on which alone a person may be detained without trial. If a person is detained on any ground other than those prescribed in the section, the preventive action will obviously be not in accordance with the law. The order of detention is plainly, on the face of it, purported to be made in the interest of public safety and the maintenance of public order. The Act nowhere sets out the same as a specific ground for preventive detention. I am, therefore, of the opinion that on its very face the impugned order of detention does not fall within the scope and ambit of section 3(1) of the Act. 

 42. The view I have taken finds support from the decision in the case of Mrs. Tahera Chowdhury Vs. The Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh, 40 DLR 193. In that case an order of detention under section 3(1)(a) of the Act as in the instant case simply stated that it was made in the interest of public safety without mentioning that the detention of the detenu was considered necessary with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act. A question arose whether such an order was legal. A Division Bench of this Court answered it in the following terms: 

 "Section 3 of the Special Powers Act provides very expressly that the Government may, if satisfied with respect to any person that with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act it is necessary so to do, make an order directing that such person be detained. Thus it is absolutely clear that section 3 of the Special Powers Act only empowers the Government to direct detention of a person only if it is satisfied that with a view to prevent him from doing any prejudicial act it is necessary to make his detention. Annexure 'A' the detention order nowhere mentions that the detention of the detenu was considered necessary to prevent him from doing any prejudicial act. Thus on the face of the order itself it is found to be without any legal authority in view of the provision of section 3 of the Special Powers Act. 

 "the said order of detention gives the only ground for detention saying that detention order is considered necessary in the interest of public safety. There is no provision for making a detention order merely, in the interest of public safety throughout the Special Powers Act." 

 43. I now tuna to the grounds of detention in order to objectively analyse whether those have any rational connection with the object mentioned in section 3(1) of the Act. Paragraph 1 of the grounds alleged that the people had pent-up wrath against the detenu for his corruption and misuse of power and so when the erstwhile President made an announcement of his resignation or 4th December, 1990 a large number of people came out in streets and attacked the persons and the institutions connected with the previous Government for which there was apprehension for the security of the life of the detenu. Paragraph 2 alleged that the detenu in his private interview with the journalist of "Morning Sun" on 8th December, 1990 made certain statement about the future of Jatiya Party and about his politics and when the said statement was published a section of the public became incited and being so enraged they damaged the house of the detenu by cocktail burst on 10th December, 1990 and had he been present in the house his life would have been at stake. Paragraph 3 alleged that as the detenu went underground there was dissatisfaction and hatred in the minds of the public as a result of which there was apprehension of serious disruption of public safety and public order. The last paragraph alleged that on consideration of the said circumstances and the situation prevailing in the country it appeared to the satisfaction of the Government that the detention of the detenu was necessary in the interest of the public safety and the maintenance of public order. 

 44. In none of the said paragraphs it is alleged that the detenu indulged himself in any activity endangering public safety and the maintenance of public order. The grounds, read as a whole, on the other hand, indicate that it was a section of the public which having had resentment in its mind against the detenu for his corruption and abuse of power was out to attack him and his property resulting in the breach of law and order for which it was necessary to give him protection from such attack. Section 3(1) of the Act confers on the Government the power to detain an individual for the purpose of preventing him from doing one or other of the 8 prejudicial acts mentioned in section 2(f)(1) to (viii) of the Act and for no other purpose. To keep a particular individual in detention for the purpose of protecting him from the onslaught of others is not contemplated within the four corners of the said provision. 

 45. In the affidavit-in-opposition it is, however, averred that the detenu has a strong background of political capability and such capability is sufficient enough to utilise entrenched support available to the Jatiya Party and the earlier regime in the administration and other areas to destabilise the present situation and thereby it can endanger public safety and public order for which detention was considered necessary with a view to preserving and protecting the public safety and public order. No such ground appears to have been stated in the document communicated to the detenu under section 8 of the Special Powers Act and the detenu had also no opportunity to make any representation in respect thereof. So the Government cannot now fall upon the same to defend its preventive action. Apart from that, the detenu might have a capability to create problems to public safety and public order, but that by itself cannot be the basis for passing an order of detention so long as he does not indulge himself in any prejudicial act endangering public safety and public order and the members of the public are not affected by his activities. 

 46. In that view of the matter I find that the object of the detention does not fall within the scope of section 3(1) of the Act. There is also no other provision of law which authorises the Government to make an order for preventive detention of a particular individual. Article 32 of the Constitution enjoins that no person shall be deprived of personal liberty save in accordance with law. As the order of detention is found to be not covered by any law, the impugned action must be held to be violative of the said constitutional mandate. 

 47. In the view I have taken it is not necessary for me to go into the question whether there is any material basis for the impugned order of detention or not.
